title: Endovascular Iliac Revascularization to Improve Diastolic Function in Patients with HFpEF and Peripheral Artery Disease (HFpAD)
summary:
In one particular form of heart failure the heart still pumps strongly enough, but can no longer relax and fill properly between beats. Those affected become short of breath quickly and tire easily. So far there are few good treatments for it.

Many of these people also have narrowed arteries in the pelvis. Such narrowings increase the resistance the heart has to pump against. We suspect that they therefore worsen not only the blood supply to the legs but also the ability of the heart to relax. Early observations suggest that heart function improves when the narrowing is widened using a catheter. This is not yet known for certain.

This study looks at 66 patients who have both conditions and in whom widening the pelvic artery is medically necessary anyway. Chance decides whether this procedure is carried out straight away or only after three months. All participants receive the procedure; only the timing differs. After three months, ultrasound is used in all participants to measure how well the heart fills. This allows a comparison of whether the group treated earlier does better.

Walking distance, a blood value reflecting strain on the heart, and how participants feel are also recorded.

interventions.name: Immediate endovascular therapy: Endovascular therapy of the symptomatic, haemodynamically relevant aorto-iliac stenosis is performed within days after randomization, in addition to guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure and blood pressure. Assessments take place at screening/baseline,

Delayed endovascular therapy: Guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure and blood pressure is continued unchanged for 90 days. Endovascular therapy is performed immediately after assessment of the primary endpoint on day 90. The procedure may be brought forward at any time for clinical re

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
I1. High-grade, symptomatic aorto-iliac artery stenosis eligible for endovascular therapy, defined as a peak systolic velocity ratio ≥ 3 in the iliac arteries or, if not quantifiable, a monophasic waveform in the common femoral artery, with Rutherford-Becker category 1-3.
I2. Established HFpEF, defined as an H2FPEF score ≥ 6 and an E/e' ratio ≥ 15 after at least four weeks of optimized medical therapy.
I3. Written informed consent.
Exclusion criteria:
E1. Foreseeable inability to achieve technical success of endovascular therapy, as judged by the treating team.
E2. Concomitant, non-treatable high-grade femoropopliteal stenosis or occlusion.
E3. Uncontrolled arterial hypertension (office systolic blood pressure > 160 mmHg).
E4. Presence of any cardiomyopathy (e.g. amyloidosis).
E5. Persistent or permanent atrial fibrillation (paroxysmal atrial fibrillation is eligible).
E6. At least moderate-to-severe valvular heart disease.
E7. Pulmonary hypertension other than type 2.
E8. Lack of capacity to provide informed consent.
E9. Severe renal impairment (eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73 m2) or dialysis.
E10. Congestive heart failure within the preceding 4 weeks (hospitalization for heart failure, ambulatory intravenous loop diuretic therapy, or at least a doubling of the oral loop diuretic dose).
E11. Severe anemia (hemoglobin < 8 g/dL) or clinically relevant coagulopathy.
E12. Estimated life expectancy < 1 year.
E13. Known severe allergy to iodinated contrast media.
E14. Inability to comply with study visits or follow-up procedures.
E15. Clinical indication for immediate revascularization (e.g. chronic limb-threatening ischemia, rest pain or tissue loss [Rutherford >= 4], acutely or rapidly progressive symptoms, or any other situation in which, in the judgment of the treating vascular team, delaying the intervention would not be justifiable).
